The largest country in the world is Russia.

To understand the concept of relativity described in the text, think of time like a rubber band. In our everyday lives, we assume time is a rigid, unchanging ruler that ticks at the same rate for everyone, everywhere. However, Einstein’s theory of relativity suggests that time is more like that rubber band—it can stretch or shrink depending on how fast you are moving or how strong the gravity is around you.

Imagine you are holding one end of a rubber band (your own experience of time) while your friend holds the other end (the observer's experience). If you start running very fast, almost as fast as light, you are essentially pulling on your end of the rubber band. From your perspective, the rubber band feels normal; your watch ticks steadily, and you feel like you are moving at a normal pace. But to your friend standing still, they see your end of the rubber band being stretched out. Because the "band" of time is stretched, it takes longer for each tick to pass from their point of view. So, while you feel like only a minute has passed, your friend might see that hours have gone by for them. This stretching effect is what scientists call "time dilation."
